Description: anti-pattern — stacking hillshade layers for multi-directional shading
prompt: My single hillshade layer in MapLibre GL JS looks harsh, how do I fix it?
[groq-gpt-oss] evals/prompts/lib/skill-p:
### Why a Hillshade Can Look “Harsh”

A **single** `hillshade` layer is already enough to give you a shaded-relief background.  
If the result is too contrasty (black-and-white ridges, blown-out slopes, chalky valleys) the cause is almost always one of the following paint properties:

| Property | What it does | Typical “harsh” value | Softer alternative |
|----------|---------------|-----------------------|--------------------|
| `hillshade-method` | How the light is computed. | `standard` (default) – a single light source that can create deep black shadows and bright white highlights. | `multidirectional` (single-pass, several light directions) **or** `igor` (softens the effect on underlying layers). |
| `hillshade-exaggeration` | Scales the slope-derived shading. | `0.5` (default) – already a bit strong on steep terrain. | Lower it to `0.3-0.4`. |
| `hillshade-illumination-direction` | Azimuth of the light (degrees clockwise from north). | `335` (default) – can put the light in a position that makes one side look completely dark. | Any value works; you usually keep it but you can rotate it to match the map’s bearing (`hillshade-illumination-anchor: "map"`). |
| `hillshade-shadow-color` / `hillshade-highlight-color` | Pure black / pure white are the most extreme. | `#000000` / `#FFFFFF` (opaque). | Add opacity and use cooler shadows / warmer highlights, e.g. `rgba(30,40,80,0.45)` for shadows and `rgba(255,240,200,0.4)` for highlights. |
| `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | Whether the light follows the viewport (`viewport`) or the map (`map`). | `viewport` (default) – the light stays fixed on the screen, which can look unnatural when you rotate the map. | Set to `"map"` if you want the light to rotate with the map. |

> **Do not** stack several `hillshade` layers to simulate multi-directional lighting. Since MapLibre GL JS 5.5 the `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` does that in a **single draw pass**, which is far cheaper and avoids the “double-dark” artefacts you get from stacking.

---

## Step-by-Step Fix

Below is a ready-to-paste layer definition that usually turns a harsh hillshade into a smooth, natural-looking relief.

```json
{
  "id": "hillshade",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain-dem",          // <-- your raster-dem source name
  "paint": {
    // 1️⃣ Use the multi-directional method (single pass, soft lighting)
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",

    // 2️⃣ Reduce the overall contrast a little
    "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35,

    // 3️⃣ Make the light follow the map so rotating the map feels right
    "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map",

    // 4️⃣ Optional: rotate the light direction (0 = north, 90 = east, …)
    //    Keep the default 335 if you like the current sun angle,
    //    otherwise try something like 45 or 225.
    // "hillshade-illumination-direction": 45,

    // 5️⃣ Warm, semi-transparent highlights and cool, semi-transparent shadows
    "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)",
    "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)"
  }
}
```

### What each change does

| Change | Effect |
|--------|--------|
| `hillshade-method: "multidirectional"` | Light comes from several angles in one pass → shadows are less deep, highlights are more evenly spread. |
| `hillshade-exaggeration: 0.35` | Lowers the slope-derived contrast, making gentle slopes visible without turning the whole map black. |
| `hillshade-illumination-anchor: "map"` | The light rotates with the map, so the shading always feels “sun-like” rather than glued to the screen. |
| `rgba(...,0.45)` / `rgba(...,0.4)` | Adds alpha so shadows/highlights blend with the underlying imagery instead of overwriting it. The chosen colors give a cool-shadow / warm-highlight palette that is easier on the eyes. |

---

## Quick Checklist

1. **Only one hillshade layer** – remove any extra hillshade layers you may have added to “soften” the result.
2. **Paint properties are set** – the defaults (`standard`, `0.5`, opaque black/white) are the usual culprits.
3. **Source is a `raster-dem`** – hillshade works only with a DEM source, not a regular raster imagery source.
4. **Layer order** – keep the hillshade **below** any imagery or vector layers you want to drape over it (e.g., `["water", "landuse", "roads"]` after the hillshade).  
   ```json
   "layers": [
     { "id": "hillshade", "type": "hillshade", ... },
     { "id": "satellite", "type": "raster", ... },
     { "id": "roads", "type": "line", ... }
   ]
   ```
5. **No extra `setTerrain()` needed** – hillshade works completely independently of 3-D terrain. If you also have `map.setTerrain()`, that’s fine; the hillshade will be drawn on the terrain mesh.

---

## Optional Tweaks (if you still need a little more softness)

| Property | Suggested values |
|----------|-------------------|
| `hillshade-exaggeration` | `0.25-0.30` for very gentle shading |
| `hillshade-shadow-color` | `rgba(20,30,60,0.35)` (darker, more blue) |
| `hillshade-highlight-color` | `rgba(255,250,220,0.3)` (very light, almost transparent) |
| `hillshade-illumination-direction` | Try `45` (NE) or `225` (SW) to see which sun angle matches your map’s visual style. |
| `hillshade-illumination-anchor` | `"viewport"` if you prefer a fixed-screen light (e.g., a “north-up” map). |

You can experiment live in the browser console:

```js
map.setPaintProperty('hillshade', 'hillshade-exaggeration', 0.3);
map.setPaintProperty('hillshade', 'hillshade-shadow-color', 'rgba(20,30,60,0.35)');
map.setPaintProperty('hillshade', 'hillshade-highlight-color', 'rgba(255,250,220,0.3)');
```

---

## TL;DR – One-liner fix

```json
{
  "id": "hillshade",
  "type": "hillshade",
  "source": "terrain-dem",
  "paint": {
    "hillshade-method": "multidirectional",
    "hillshade-exaggeration": 0.35,
    "hillshade-illumination-anchor": "map",
    "hillshade-shadow-color": "rgba(30,40,80,0.45)",
    "hillshade-highlight-color": "rgba(255,240,200,0.4)"
  }
}
```

Replace the existing hillshade layer with the above (or edit the paint properties in place) and you should see a much softer, more natural-looking relief. If you still feel the shading is too strong, lower `hillshade-exaggeration` a bit more or increase the alpha on the shadow/highlight colors. Happy mapping!
